headline: AI labs and other AI developers are buying the code, emails and chat records of shut-down startups to train their models.
score_reason: Pool score 5 kept: a real and growing market with privacy stakes, but the training benefit is unproven and the deal figures come from the brokers.
importance_line: Former employees' emails and messages can end up as AI training material, and Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University, says no federal law bans such sales, but founders cannot see who buys the data and no one has shown that real company data trains better AI.
summary: MIT Technology Review reports that firms such as SimpleClosure and Sunset, which help failing startups wind down, are now selling those startups' code and workplace data (emails, chats and documents) to AI labs and other model builders, with SimpleClosure saying 47 percent of its deals now include a code or data sale. No company has yet published tests showing that real company data trains better AI than the alternatives, the legal and privacy position is unsettled (Spirit Airlines' flight attendants' union objected to Google's $10 million purchase of the bankrupt airline's data), and the proceeds typically go to creditors and investors rather than employees.
notes: Read in full. Trend piece rather than a single-day event; the industry started in April 2026 and the Spirit Airlines sale was in Aug 2026.
